title: Security Design Principles
summary: The Saltzer & Schroeder-style principles that make a design inherently harder to get wrong, independent of any specific control — from Kerckhoffs's principle to fail-safe defaults.

slides.markdown:
Every security control eventually gets old, broken, or bypassed. What survives is the **design philosophy** underneath it — a small set of engineering principles, formalized by Saltzer and Schroeder in 1975, that make a system harder to get wrong regardless of which specific controls you bolt on.

These aren't abstract theory. "Assume the attacker knows your design," "check every access, not just the first one," "fail closed, not open" — these are the exact reasons a well-built firewall rule set, auth middleware, or crypto library looks the way it does.

Interviewers ask about these principles directly because they separate people who've internalized *why* security designs look the way they do from people who've only memorized *what* the designs are.

slides.subTitle: Assume the design is public
slides.markdown:
Formulated by Auguste Kerckhoffs in 1883 for cipher design, but it applies to every security system: **a system should be secure even if everything about it — except the key — is known to the attacker.**

Why this is the right assumption rather than a pessimistic one: designs leak. Employees leave, code gets decompiled, vendors get breached, papers get published. Any security that depends on the attacker *not knowing how it works* has an expiration date you don't control and can't detect crossing.

What should stay secret instead is narrow and manageable: **keys, passwords, and specific credentials** — things you can rotate. Modern cryptography takes this to its logical conclusion: AES and RSA are fully public specifications, reviewed by thousands of researchers, and their security rests entirely on the secrecy of the key, not the algorithm.

slides.sectionTitle: Why obscurity fails as a sole control
slides.markdown:
"Security through obscurity" means relying on secrecy of the design itself — an undocumented API endpoint, a custom (unreviewed) crypto scheme, a hidden admin path — rather than on a control that holds up under Kerckhoffs's assumption.

Three concrete reasons it fails as the *only* layer:

- **It doesn't survive discovery**, and discovery is cheap: a hidden endpoint shows up in a JS bundle, a network trace, or a directory brute-force in seconds.
- **It can't be audited.** A reviewer can verify "this key is 256 bits and unguessable." Nobody can verify "this is well hidden" — hiddenness isn't a property you can measure or test.
- **It gives false confidence**, which is often worse than no control at all — teams skip real access control because they believe the obscurity is doing the job.

Obscurity isn't worthless as an *extra* layer (an unlisted admin URL still filters out casual scanning) — the failure is treating it as sufficient on its own instead of layering it on top of real authentication and authorization.

slides.subTitle: Simplicity is a security property
slides.markdown:
**Economy of mechanism**: keep the design as small and simple as the requirements allow. Every line of code, every configuration option, every code path is a place a bug — and therefore a vulnerability — can hide.

This shows up concretely in security-critical code:

- A parser with fewer branches is easier to reason about for every input, including adversarial ones — most memory-corruption CVEs live in complex parsing logic (image codecs, protocol decoders) precisely because complexity hides the edge case nobody tested.
- A permission model with three roles is auditable by a human; one with forty overlapping, inherited roles is not — nobody can confidently answer "who can do X" anymore, which is itself a security failure.
- Authentication libraries deliberately expose a tiny surface (`hash`, `verify`) rather than every internal primitive, so there's less to misuse.

The rule of thumb: if you can't explain a security-relevant piece of your system in a few sentences, it's probably too complex to reason about correctly — and an attacker only needs one path you didn't reason about.

slides.subTitle: Check every access, every time
slides.markdown:
**Complete mediation**: every single access to every resource must be checked against the current permission state — not just the first request in a session, and not against a cached decision from a minute ago.

The classic violation is a **time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU)** gap: a system checks "can this user read file X" once at login, caches "yes," and then serves every subsequent request from that cache — even after an admin has since revoked access. Between the check and the use, the world changed, and the cache didn't notice.

This is why:

- Session tokens are checked against a live permission store (or a short-lived, frequently refreshed claim), not a permission snapshot taken at login.
- File systems re-check permissions on every `open()` call, not once per process.
- API gateways authorize *per request*, even for a client that authenticated seconds earlier.

The cost is real — a permission check on every request is more expensive than one cached check — and complete mediation says pay it anyway, because a stale "yes" is a live vulnerability.

slides.subTitle: Baked in, not bolted on
slides.markdown:
**Fail-safe defaults**: the default state of any access decision should be **deny**, and access is granted only by explicit rule — never the reverse.

The distinction that matters: this has to be the *design's default*, not a rule someone remembers to add later. "Deny unless explicitly allowed" baked into the authorization framework means a developer who forgets to write a rule for a new resource gets a safe outcome (403) automatically. "Allow unless explicitly denied" bolted on top means the same forgetful developer just shipped an open resource, and nothing in the system will tell them.

Concrete instances: a firewall's default policy should be `DROP`, not `ACCEPT`; a new IAM role should start with zero permissions, not full access minus a blocklist; an error in an authorization check should resolve to "deny" — a bug that throws an exception should never accidentally grant access because the code that would have denied it never ran.

The test for whether a system truly has fail-safe defaults: does a missing rule, a crash, or a forgotten configuration line make things *more* locked down, or *less*?

Two related but distinct principles, both about not concentrating power in one place:

- **Separation of privilege** — a sensitive action should require more than one condition to be true, not a single credential. Sudo access plus a hardware key, or a database migration that needs both a valid deploy token *and* running from an approved CI pipeline, means compromising one factor isn't enough.
- **Separation of duty** — a sensitive *action* should require more than one *person*. The engineer who writes a production database migration shouldn't be the same one who approves and merges it; a person authorized to initiate a wire transfer shouldn't also be the person who approves it. This is why financial systems have a "maker-checker" pattern and why cloud IAM commonly restricts who can both create and approve their own access changes.

Both exist for the same reason least privilege does: they shrink the blast radius of a single compromised credential or a single insider, forcing collusion or a compound failure instead of one mistake.

slides.subTitle: Security people won't route around
slides.markdown:
**Psychological acceptability**: if a security control is significantly more annoying than the workaround, people will find the workaround — and that workaround is usually less secure than the control it replaced.

Real examples every engineer has seen:

- A password policy that forces a new 16-character password every 30 days reliably produces sticky notes on monitors and passwords incremented by one digit (`Summer2024!` → `Summer2025!`) — the policy made memorization impossible, so people wrote it down or made it predictable instead.
- A VPN that's slow or unreliable for legitimate work pushes engineers toward personal devices or unsanctioned file-sharing tools that IT has zero visibility into.
- An approval workflow with a two-day SLA on an urgent production fix gets bypassed by someone with standing access, defeating the separation of duty it was meant to enforce.

The design implication: a control's *usability* is not a nice-to-have layered on top of its security — a control nobody can tolerate using is a control that gets circumvented, which makes it net-negative for security, not neutral.

slides.sectionTitle: Open design vs obscurity, side by side
slides.markdown:
| | Open design (Kerckhoffs) | Obscurity as sole control |
|---|---|---|
| **What's secret** | Only the key/credential | The design itself |
| **Survives discovery** | Yes — discovery of the algorithm changes nothing | No — discovery is often total compromise |
| **Auditable** | Yes — a third party can verify the key space and math | No — "well hidden" isn't a testable property |
| **Example** | AES, RSA: public algorithms, secret keys | A custom unreviewed cipher; a hidden but unauthenticated admin endpoint |
| **Failure mode** | A key leaks — rotate it | The design leaks — the whole control is gone, nothing to rotate |

The practical takeaway isn't "never use anything hidden" — an unlisted endpoint or an unpublished internal API is fine as a *minor* deterrent. The takeaway is that anything carrying real risk needs a control that is still secure under Kerckhoffs's assumption, with obscurity, if used at all, only as an extra thin layer on top.

slides.sectionTitle: "Nobody knows how it works" is not "it's secure"
slides.markdown:
The pitfall these principles guard against, stated directly: confusing **the design is not publicly known** with **the design is secure**.

These are unrelated claims. A homegrown authentication scheme that nobody outside the team has seen isn't secure because it's obscure — it's *unvalidated*. It hasn't survived the scrutiny that finds the flaws: no cryptographer has tried to break it, no red team has probed it, no bug bounty has been paid against it. "Nobody has found a flaw" and "there is no flaw" are very different statements when the number of people looking is zero.

This is precisely why the security community treats **peer review as a prerequisite**, not a formality — public algorithms like AES beat every credible cryptanalysis attempt for over two decades specifically *because* they were public and attacked by the best researchers in the world, not despite it. An obscure scheme skips that gauntlet entirely, and the absence of scrutiny is not evidence of strength.

These principles aren't independent trivia — they compose into one coherent stance: **assume the attacker is smart, patient, and knows everything except your secrets, then build so that a single mistake doesn't cascade.**

A well-designed permission system demonstrates several at once: it's simple enough to audit (economy of mechanism), denies by default (fail-safe defaults), re-checks on every request (complete mediation), doesn't rely on anyone not finding the admin panel (Kerckhoffs), and is usable enough that engineers don't route around it (psychological acceptability).

When asked to critique a design in an interview, naming *which principle* a flaw violates — not just "this seems insecure" — is what signals depth: "this caches the auth decision at login, which violates complete mediation" is a much stronger answer than "this could be exploited." The next topics in this group — defense-in-depth, threat modeling, risk frameworks — are where these principles turn into a repeatable process.
